 Retirement Original Medicare vs. Medicare Advantage: A 7-point checklist for 2027 enrollment 
 Published Oct 22, 2026 | Time to read 8 min Andrew Kessel Editorial staff, J.P. Morgan Wealth Management
 When it comes to Medicare and Medicare Advantage plans, healthcare networks and access can change year to year. Before you renew your plan, check whether your doctors, hospitals and preferred facilities are still covered.
 Don’t autorenew on premium alone. Compare plans based on total annual cost and what you could pay in a higher-use year.
 Price your prescriptions. Changes to drug tiers, preferred pharmacies and rules like prior authorization can affect a plan’s cost and convenience.
 Open enrollment for Medicare and Medicare Advantage runs October 15 to December 7 every year. During this window, enrollees can elect to keep or change their coverage for the year ahead.
 If you’re already enrolled, it can be tempting to let your plan autorenew. But Medicare coverage can change from year to year in ways that affect what you pay and where you can receive care, so it may be worth taking a fresh look before simply sticking with what you have.
 Here’s what you should know about the different types of plans and what to consider when selecting or renewing one.
 Medicare vs. Medicare Advantage
 At a high level, your choice usually comes down to original (or traditional) Medicare versus Medicare Advantage. Original Medicare comprises Part A (hospital stays) and Part B (doctor visits), plus the optional Part D (prescription drug coverage). Enrollees can buy additional coverage, known as Medigap, to cover some out-of-pocket costs. 
 Medicare Advantage – also known as Part C – is offered by private insurers and typically combines Part A, Part B and often Part D. Plans may also provide access to dental and vision benefits, which original Medicare does not; however, those benefits are more likely to require referrals or prior authorization.
 People who prefer Medicare tend to like that they can see any Medicare provider in the U.S. and typically don’t need a referral to see a specialist. People who prefer Medicare Advantage may appreciate the convenience of a bundled plan and are often looking for lower premiums, even if care options are limited by a provider’s network.
 The checks outlined below can help you compare your options with fewer surprises.

 Check 1: Provider access and networks (do my doctors/hospitals stay in network?)
 The first thing to check when you’re considering switching plans is whether you’ll still have access to the doctors and hospitals you trust.
 If you have Medicare, ask providers whether they accept it. If they don’t, you may be billed more than the amount approved by Medicare.
 If you’re currently enrolled in a Medicare Advantage or a Part D plan, you will likely have received an Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) breaking down any changes to coverage and costs for 2027. For example, the maximum out-of-pocket cost (more on that below) for a Medicare Part D plan will increase from $2,100 in 2026 to $2,400 in 2027. ANOCs are typically required to be delivered by September 30, so call your plan provider if you haven’t received one.
 It’s important to confirm whether a specific provider is in network; however, knowing a doctor is in network with your insurer doesn’t guarantee they take every plan that insurer offers.
 Check 2: Total annual costs, beyond the premium
 Medicare Advantage costs can be easier to estimate when you separate fixed costs from usage costs and stress-test the plan for a high-use year. A low, or even $0, premium looks great on paper, but it’s critical to understand how much using your plan will actually cost.
 Most Medicare Advantage members pay the standard Medicare Part B monthly premium, which for 2027 is estimated to be $209.50, according to the Medicare Boards of Trustees. This premium is typically deducted from Social Security. Some Medicare Advantage plans have an additional premium, while others do not.
 Then there are the variable costs. Confirm your deductible, plus the copayments for primary care, specialists, imaging, urgent care, emergency room visits and hospital stays. These numbers can usually be found in a plan’s summary of benefits. For any prescription drugs you’re currently taking, check your plan documents for pricing.
 Using those details, you may be able to estimate costs for a typical year of care. Maybe that’s a few specialist visits, one or two prescription drugs, and one imaging appointment. But it’s also important to estimate a year where you might need more care, factoring in things like an unexpected surgery or extended hospital stay.
 Medicare Advantage has a maximum out-of-pocket cost for covered medical services, while original Medicare doesn’t. For that reason, many beneficiaries of original Medicare opt to also enroll in Medigap, a supplemental insurance that can reduce out-of-pocket costs.
 Note that an additional income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA) can increase your costs if your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is above certain thresholds. IRMAA is determined using your tax return from two years prior, so the 2027 figure will be set based on your 2025 return. This can lead to an unexpected cost increase for some enrollees because it includes one-time income events, such as IRA withdrawals, Roth conversions or exercising equity-based compensation.
 Check 3: Prescription drug coverage
 Even when Medicare Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan covers a medication, your out-of-pocket cost can shift materially based on which tier it’s assigned to, which pharmacy you use, and whether the plan requires prior authorization or step therapy.
 Generally, people pay monthly for prescription drugs depending on their cost tier. Lower tiers tend to include generics and preferred brands, while higher tiers include nonpreferred brands and specialty drugs. Because plans can move a drug to a different tier, it’s worth checking your exact drugs and dosages each year. Some plans may require you to try one or more lower-tier drugs before covering a higher-tier drug, a practice known as step therapy.
 Prices may also depend on whether you’re using a preferred pharmacy. Confirm that your preferred pharmacy is still the same, and if you’ve moved in the past year, check whether another preferred location is in your area.
 Check 4: MOOP cost – what it does and doesn’t cap
 Medicare Advantage plans cap payments at a maximum out-of-pocket (MOOP) cost, which can keep bills from spiraling out of control if you need more medical care than expected.
 A couple of things to note: First, some plans don’t count drug costs toward your MOOP cost, so be sure to check. Second, a plan may have a higher MOOP cost for out-of-network providers.
 With original Medicare, there is no limit on what you could pay out of pocket. This is where Medigap comes in. Medigap plans, offered by private insurers, cost a monthly premium and cover some of the copayments, coinsurance and deductibles that Medicare does not. There is a range of Medigap options, and choosing a higher premium will generally get you a lower deductible and more covered costs.
 This is one of the key trade-offs of Medicare versus Medicare Advantage. Under Medicare and Medigap, your costs may be higher month to month but are generally more predictable.
 Check 5: Coverage away from home
 If you travel frequently or split time between states, you’ll want to know where your plan is in network.
 With original Medicare, the question is typically whether a provider accepts Medicare, regardless of region. This can make coverage feel more portable.
 Medicare Advantage plans sometimes rely on local or regional networks for non-emergency care, potentially limiting your options or raising your costs away from home. If you want a specific out-of-state hospital system to be covered, make sure to verify.
 Check 6: Stability risk and coverage disruption
 Because Medicare Advantage plans are offered by private insurers, those companies can – and sometimes do – elect to stop offering certain plans altogether. That means you may be required to find new insurance for 2027 even if you hadn’t intended to switch.
 This has become more common. Last year, roughly 10% of people enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan were forced to move to another plan or opt for traditional Medicare for 2026, compared with about 7% for 2025 and just 1% on average from 2018 to 2024. 
 If your plan has been disrupted, you should have been notified by your insurer prior to the start of open enrollment, and you may have an extended special enrollment period to make a new selection.
 Check 7: What’s changed for you?
 Your insurance plan may not have changed, but what you need from a plan may feel different now than it did a year ago.
 You may have added a new specialist, started or stopped a medication, scheduled a procedure, or noticed you’re using care more or less than you expected. Lifestyle changes – such as moving, traveling more or choosing to split your time between homes – can also affect which option makes the most sense.
 These personal changes should frame how you think about checks 1–6 when evaluating your plan options.
 The bottom line
 Think of open enrollment as an annual checkup for your Medicare coverage. Before you autorenew, review your ANOC and rerun the basics using your current reality (doctors, prescriptions, travel plans and expected care).
 The goal of these checks is to answer the following questions:
 Will my providers still be in network?
 Have there been changes to my premium, cost sharing or MOOP cost?
 Has my prescription coverage (tiers, pharmacies or rules) changed?
 Have the prior authorization or referral policies changed?
 Is my network limited if I travel or split time between homes?
 Have my vision or dental benefits changed?
 What are my care needs and priorities for the year ahead?
 Whether you’re choosing coverage for the first time or considering a renewal, it’s important to select a plan that fits your priorities around doctor and hospital access, total annual cost and prescription coverage.
 Frequently asked questions about Medicare and Medicare Advantage 
 Should I expect to switch plans every year? 
 Not necessarily. If your doctors and prescriptions are still covered and your needs haven’t materially changed, staying put can be perfectly reasonable. The key is to make renewal a deliberate choice after a quick review, rather than an automatic one.
 Can I have Medicare Advantage and Medigap at the same time? 
 Generally, no. Medigap is designed to work with original Medicare, not Medicare Advantage. If you enroll in Medicare Advantage, you typically wouldn’t use Medigap to cover that plan’s copays or coinsurance.
 If I switch from Medicare and Medigap to Medicare Advantage, can I switch back later? 
 Possibly, but this is an important area to understand before you make a change. In many states, if you later decide to leave Medicare Advantage and reapply for a Medigap policy, you may be subject to medical underwriting, which can mean higher premiums or a denial of coverage depending on your health and the insurer’s rules. There are exceptions (often called “guaranteed issue” rights) in certain situations and time windows, but they’re not universal.
 If you’re eligible for Medigap, you may want to consider starting with it when you first enroll in Medicare, because that initial enrollment period is often when Medigap coverage is easiest to obtain. If you’re considering switching, it can be worth confirming what your Medigap options would be if you ever wanted to return to original Medicare in the future (and how your state rules apply).
